title: HER STORY WASN’T CLEAN.
paragraphs: HER STORY WASN’T CLEAN.

Not polished.
Not predictable.
Not Sunday-school safe.
And yet… her name is written in the bloodline of Jesus.
Open your Bible to Book of Genesis 38. Then turn to Gospel of Matthew 1:3.
You’ll find a woman most people would rather skip.
Tamar.

Judah takes her as a wife for his son.
The son dies in wickedness before God.

Another son is given to her.
He refuses to give her a child.
He dies too.

Now Tamar is a widow. Twice.
Childless. Blamed. Forgotten.

And Judah? He withholds the third son.
Leaves her suspended in shame.
Pause.
In that culture, childlessness wasn’t just grief — it was social death. No security. No future. No covering.
Tamar is trapped inside a system that failed her.
So she does something desperate.
She removes her widow’s garments. Covers herself with a veil. Sits by the roadside.
Judah — yes, Judah — sleeps with her, not knowing who she is.
Scandal explodes when she’s found pregnant.
Judah thunders: “Bring her out! Let her be burned!”
But Tamar sends back the seal, the cord, and the staff.
The receipts.
“The father belongs to the man who owns these.”
Silence.
Judah’s words cut the air:
“She is more righteous than I.”
Let that sink in.
The woman everyone would label immoral is declared righteous over a patriarch.
Why?

Not because deception is holy.
Not because manipulation is blessed.
But because Tamar was fighting for the covenant promise Judah failed to protect.
Some scholars interpret her act as a bold pursuit of levirate justice in a broken patriarchal system. Others wrestle with the ethics of her strategy. Scripture doesn’t romanticize it.
But it does something louder.
It preserves her name.
Fast forward.
Gospel of Matthew 1:3 — “Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar…”

Not erased.
Not hidden.
Not footnoted.
Named.
Four women appear in that genealogy. Each story carries scandal. Each carries irregularity. And God doesn’t sanitize any of them.
Why would the Holy Spirit highlight Tamar in the Messiah’s lineage?
Because Jesus didn’t come from a spotless family tree.
He came through it.

Through betrayal.
Through hypocrisy.
Through sexual sin.
Through injustice.
And He came for people inside those very things.
Listen carefully.

Tamar’s story isn’t about endorsing scandal.
It’s about exposing our need for redemption.
Judah would later father a line that leads to King David… and ultimately to Christ.
But in Genesis 38, Judah is not heroic.
He is compromised.
And yet God weaves even compromised men and wounded women into His redemptive tapestry.
That’s grace.

Not excusing sin.
Not ignoring wrongdoing.
But overruling brokenness with sovereign mercy.
Here’s the Gospel turn.
We are all in Genesis 38 somewhere.

We’ve been sinned against.
We’ve sinned ourselves.
We’ve made desperate moves.
We’ve hidden behind veils.
But Jesus — the Lion of the tribe of Judah — stepped into that very bloodline to carry the shame.
On the cross, He bore the weight of every distorted story.

Your secret.
Your regret.
Your “if only.”
He doesn’t whitewash your past.
He redeems it.
Tamar gave birth to Perez — which means “breakthrough.”
Through a scandalous chapter, God birthed a breakthrough that carried the Messiah forward.
Hear me.
Your worst chapter is not the final author of your destiny.
Christ is.

Repent where you’ve sinned.
Trust Him where you’ve been wounded.
Lay down the veil.
Bring the receipts of your brokenness to the cross.
Because the same grace that wrote Tamar into Matthew 1 is still writing today.
